questions.q: In the measurement of viscosity of liquids using terminal velocity experiment, spherical balls of same radius but having different densities are used. The variation of the terminal velocity ($v$) with the ratio of density of spherical ball ($\sigma$) to density of the liquid ($\rho$), is best represented by :
questions.solution:
The terminal velocity $v$ of a spherical ball of radius $r$ and density $\sigma$ falling through a liquid of density $\rho$ and viscosity $\eta$ is given by Stokes' law:

$v = \dfrac{2r^2g}{9\eta}(\sigma - \rho)$

Rearranging the terms to express $v$ as a function of the ratio $\dfrac{\sigma}{\rho}$:

$v = \dfrac{2r^2g\rho}{9\eta} \left( \dfrac{\sigma}{\rho} - 1 \right)$

Let $y = v$ and $x = \dfrac{\sigma}{\rho}$. The equation becomes:

$y = k(x - 1)$

where $k = \dfrac{2r^2g\rho}{9\eta}$ is a positive constant.

This represents the equation of a straight line with a positive slope $k$ and an x-intercept at $x = 1$ (i.e., $v = 0$ when $\dfrac{\sigma}{\rho} = 1$).

Looking at the given graphs, only the second graph shows a straight line with a positive slope that intersects the horizontal axis at $\dfrac{\sigma}{\rho} = 1$.

questions.q:
A submarine is designed to withstand an absolute pressure of $100$ atm. How deep can it go below the water surface ?
(Consider the density of water $= 1000$ kg m$^{-3}$, $1$ atm $= 1 \times 10^{5}$ Pa and gravitational acceleration $g = 10$ m/s$^2$)
questions.solution:
The absolute pressure at a depth $h$ below the water surface is given by $P = P_0 + \rho g h$, where $P_0$ is the atmospheric pressure.

Given:
$P = 100$ atm $= 100 \times 10^5$ Pa
$P_0 = 1$ atm $= 1 \times 10^5$ Pa
$\rho = 1000$ kg m$^{-3}$
$g = 10$ m/s$^2$

Substituting the values into the equation:

$100 \times 10^5 = 1 \times 10^5 + 1000 \times 10 \times h$

$99 \times 10^5 = 10^4 \times h$

$h = \dfrac{99 \times 10^5}{10^4}$

$h = 990$ m

Answer: $990$ m

questions.q: Water rises to a height 'h' in capillary tube. If the length of capillary tube above the surface of water is made less than 'h', then:
options: water rises upto the top of capillary tube and stays there without overflowing.
water rises upto a point a little below the top and stays there.
water does not rise at all.
water rises upto the tip of capillary tube and then starts overflowing like a fountain.
questions.solution: It won't overflow. That should be obvious since doing so would create a constant flow, constantly using energy, but without any energy input. The same force that pulls the water along the inside of the capillary tube also holds it there when it reaches the end. This force doesn't just pull upward, it pulls the water along the glass. At a certain height, the weight of the water column balances this pull. In that case the pull is upward since there is water below but not above.

questions.q:
Water flows in a streamline motion through a horizontal pipe of circular cross-section as shown in the figure. The pressure difference of water between $P$ and $Q$ is $15$ Nm$^{-2}$. The area of cross-section at $P$ and $Q$ are $40$ cm$^2$ and $20$ cm$^2$, respectively. The rate of flow of water through the pipe, in cm$^3$s$^{-1}$, is :
[Take density of water $=1000$ kg m$^{-3}$]
questions.solution:
From the equation of continuity, the rate of flow is constant:

$A_P v_P = A_Q v_Q$

Given $A_P = 40 \text{ cm}^2$ and $A_Q = 20 \text{ cm}^2$, we have:

$40 v_P = 20 v_Q \Rightarrow v_Q = 2 v_P$

Applying Bernoulli's equation for a horizontal pipe:

$P_P + \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v_P^2 = P_Q + \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v_Q^2$

$P_P - P_Q = \dfrac{1}{2} \rho (v_Q^2 - v_P^2)$

Substitute the given values ($P_P - P_Q = 15 \text{ N m}^{-2}$, $\rho = 1000 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$) and $v_Q = 2 v_P$:

$15 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1000 \times ((2 v_P)^2 - v_P^2)$

$15 = 500 \times (4 v_P^2 - v_P^2)$

$15 = 500 \times 3 v_P^2$

$15 = 1500 v_P^2$

$v_P^2 = \dfrac{1}{100} \Rightarrow v_P = 0.1 \text{ m s}^{-1} = 10 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$

The rate of flow of water is:

$Q = A_P v_P = 40 \text{ cm}^2 \times 10 \text{ cm s}^{-1} = 400 \text{ cm}^3 \text{ s}^{-1}$

Answer: $400$

Statement (B): Water does not wet an oily glass because cohesive force of oil is less than that of water.

options: A. B. and C are false

A and B false,
C is true
B and C false, A is true
A and C false, B is true
questions.solution:
Statement A:

In liquid: With the rise in temperature, viscosity of a liquid decreases because the intermolecular attractive force between consecutive layers decreases as temperature increases. 

In gasses: The important cause of viscosity is randomness/molecular collision due to root mean square velocity. Due to rise in temperature, kinetic energy of molecules increases which makes rms velocity increase, hence randomness and collision of molecules increases. This makes the flow difficult and hence viscosity in gasses increases with temperature.

Statement B:

Water does not wet an oily glass, because  cohesive force for water > adhesive force between water and oil molecules.

Statement C:

When the liquid does not wet the sides of a solid object, it means that the angle of contact is more than 90° but less than 180°.

We use Torricelli's theorem for efflux speed: \(v=\sqrt{2 g h}\)

options: i \(\rightarrow\) B, ii \(\rightarrow\) A, iii \(\rightarrow\) A, iv \(\rightarrow\) B
i \(\rightarrow\) A, ii \(\rightarrow A\), iii \(\rightarrow B\), iv \(\rightarrow B\)
i \(\rightarrow\) A, ii \(\rightarrow\) B, iii \(\rightarrow\) A, iv \(\rightarrow B\)
i \(\rightarrow\) B, ii \(\rightarrow\) A, iii \(\rightarrow\) B, iv \(\rightarrow\) A
questions.solution:
Case (i): \(a_x=0, a_y \neq 0\)
- Vertical acceleration only \(\rightarrow\) pressure distribution changes with depth only, not horizontally.
- So, \(P_A=P_B\).
\(\rightarrow\) Matches A.
Case (ii): \(a_x=0, a_y=0\)
- No acceleration \(\rightarrow\) normal hydrostatic condition.
- Same level \(\Rightarrow\) same pressure.
- So, \(P_A=P_B\).
\(\rightarrow\) Matches A.
Case (iii): \(a_x\gt 0, a_y=0\)
- Accelerating in \(+x \Rightarrow\) pressure increases opposite to acceleration (left side has higher pressure).
- A is on left, B on right \(\Rightarrow P_A\gt P_B\).
\(\rightarrow\) Matches B.
Case (iv): \(a_x\gt 0, a_y\gt 0\)
- Combined acceleration: vertical affects depth, horizontal affects sidewise pressure.
- At same level, vertical component doesn't matter.
- So, still \(P_A\gt P_B\).
\(\rightarrow\) Matches B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A steady flow of an ideal fluid occurs through a horizontal pipe of varying cross-section. The kinetic energy per unit volume of the fluid at section A is $4$ times the kinetic energy per unit volume at section B. The ratio of the diameter of the pipe at section A to the diameter at section B ($d_A : d_B$) is:
questions.solution:
Kinetic energy per unit volume is given by $K = \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v^2$.

Given that $K_A = 4 K_B$, we have:
$\dfrac{1}{2} \rho v_A^2 = 4 \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v_B^2 \right)$
$v_A^2 = 4 v_B^2 \Rightarrow v_A = 2 v_B$

According to the equation of continuity, $A_A v_A = A_B v_B$.
Since the cross-sectional area $A = \dfrac{\pi d^2}{4}$, we can write:
$d_A^2 v_A = d_B^2 v_B$
$\left( \dfrac{d_A}{d_B} \right)^2 = \dfrac{v_B}{v_A} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Taking the square root on both sides, we get:
$\dfrac{d_A}{d_B} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

Thus, the ratio $d_A : d_B$ is $1 : \sqrt{2}$.

Answer: $1 : \sqrt{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A straight metal wire of length $10 \text{ cm}$ rests horizontally on the surface of water. If the surface tension of water is $0.07 \text{ N m}^{-1}$ and the acceleration due to gravity is $10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$, what is the maximum mass of the wire that can be supported by surface tension alone without sinking?
questions.solution:
For a straight wire resting on a liquid surface, the liquid is in contact with both sides of the wire's length.

Effective length of contact, $L_{\text{eff}} = 2L$

Upward force due to surface tension, $F = T \times L_{\text{eff}} = T \times 2L$

For the wire to be supported without sinking, this upward force must balance the downward weight of the wire ($W = mg$).

$mg = 2TL$

$m = \dfrac{2TL}{g}$

Given:
$T = 0.07 \text{ N m}^{-1}$
$L = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$
$g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$

$m = \dfrac{2 \times 0.07 \times 0.1}{10} = \dfrac{0.014}{10} = 0.0014 \text{ kg}$

Converting to grams:
$m = 0.0014 \times 1000 \text{ g} = 1.4 \text{ g}$

Answer: $1.4 \text{ g}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A horizontal venturimeter is used to measure the flow speed of water (density $= 1000 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$). The cross-sectional areas of the wide and narrow sections of the pipe are $30 \text{ cm}^2$ and $10 \text{ cm}^2$, respectively. A U-tube manometer connected between these two sections contains a liquid of density $5000 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$. If the height difference of the manometer liquid in the two arms is $40 \text{ cm}$, what is the flow speed of water at the wider section of the pipe?
[Take $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$]
questions.solution:
Let the flow speed at the wide section be $v_1$ and at the narrow section be $v_2$.

From the equation of continuity:

$A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$

$30 \times v_1 = 10 \times v_2 \Rightarrow v_2 = 3 v_1$

The pressure difference $\Delta P$ between the two sections is given by the manometer reading:

$\Delta P = (\rho_m - \rho_w) g h$

Substitute the given values ($\rho_m = 5000 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$, $\rho_w = 1000 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$, $h = 0.4 \text{ m}$):

$\Delta P = (5000 - 1000) \times 10 \times 0.4 = 4000 \times 4 = 16000 \text{ Pa}$

Applying Bernoulli's equation for a horizontal pipe:

$\Delta P = \dfrac{1}{2} \rho_w (v_2^2 - v_1^2)$

$16000 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1000 \times ((3 v_1)^2 - v_1^2)$

$16000 = 500 \times (9 v_1^2 - v_1^2)$

$16000 = 500 \times 8 v_1^2$

$16000 = 4000 v_1^2$

$v_1^2 = 4 \Rightarrow v_1 = 2 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Answer: $2 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A vessel in the shape of a truncated cone, which is narrower at the top and wider at the base, has a base area $A$. It is filled with a liquid of density $\rho$ up to a height $h$. If the total mass of the liquid in the vessel is $M$, how does the force $F$ exerted by the liquid on the base of the vessel compare to the true weight of the liquid $Mg$?
questions.solution:
The pressure $P$ exerted by the liquid on the base of the vessel is given by $P = \rho g h$.

The force $F$ exerted by the liquid on the base is $F = P \times A = \rho g h A$.

Because the vessel is narrower at the top and wider at the base, its actual volume $V$ is less than the volume of a cylinder with the same base area $A$ and height $h$ (i.e., $V \lt A h$).

The total mass of the liquid is $M = \rho V$.

Since $V \lt A h$, it follows that $M \lt \rho A h$, and the true weight of the liquid is $Mg \lt \rho g h A$.

Therefore, the force exerted on the base is greater than the true weight of the liquid ($F \gt Mg$). This is a classic example of the hydrostatic paradox.

Answer: $F \gt Mg$

questions.q:
An open cylindrical vessel contains two immiscible liquids. A layer of water of height $2$ m is at the bottom, and a layer of oil of height $3$ m is on top. What is the absolute pressure at the bottom of the vessel?
(Given: density of water $= 1000$ kg m$^{-3}$, density of oil $= 800$ kg m$^{-3}$, atmospheric pressure $= 1.01 \times 10^5$ Pa, and $g = 10$ m/s$^2$)
questions.solution:
The absolute pressure at the bottom of the vessel is the sum of the atmospheric pressure and the pressure exerted by the two fluid columns.

Pressure due to the oil layer:
$P_{\text{oil}} = \rho_{\text{oil}} g h_{\text{oil}}$
$P_{\text{oil}} = 800 \times 10 \times 3 = 24,000$ Pa

Pressure due to the water layer:
$P_{\text{water}} = \rho_{\text{water}} g h_{\text{water}}$
$P_{\text{water}} = 1000 \times 10 \times 2 = 20,000$ Pa

Total gauge pressure at the bottom:
$P_{\text{gauge}} = P_{\text{oil}} + P_{\text{water}} = 24,000 + 20,000 = 44,000$ Pa $= 0.44 \times 10^5$ Pa

Absolute pressure at the bottom:
$P_{\text{abs}} = P_{\text{atm}} + P_{\text{gauge}}$
$P_{\text{abs}} = 1.01 \times 10^5 + 0.44 \times 10^5 = 1.45 \times 10^5$ Pa.

Answer: $1.45 \times 10^5$ Pa

For a solid square plate, only the outer perimeter is in contact with the liquid surface.

Total effective length of contact, $L_{\text{eff}} = 4a$, where $a$ is the side length of the plate.

Excess force required, $F = T \times L_{\text{eff}} = T \times 4a$

$12 \times 10^{-3} = 0.06 \times 4a$

$4a = \dfrac{12 \times 10^{-3}}{0.06} = 0.2\text{ m}$

$a = 0.05\text{ m} = 5\text{ cm}$

Answer: $5\text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two small solid spheres, A and B, are dropped into a tall column of a viscous fluid of density $\rho_0$. Sphere A has a radius $r$ and density $4\rho_0$. Sphere B has a radius $2r$ and density $1.5\rho_0$. The ratio of the terminal velocity of sphere A to that of sphere B ($v_A : v_B$) is:
questions.solution:
According to Stokes' law, the terminal velocity $v_t$ of a sphere of radius $R$ and density $\rho$ falling through a fluid of density $\sigma$ is given by:

$v_t = \dfrac{2}{9} \dfrac{R^2 (\rho - \sigma) g}{\eta}$

Thus, $v_t \propto R^2 (\rho - \sigma)$.

For sphere A:
$v_A \propto r^2 (4\rho_0 - \rho_0)$
$v_A \propto 3r^2\rho_0$

For sphere B:
$v_B \propto (2r)^2 (1.5\rho_0 - \rho_0)$
$v_B \propto 4r^2 (0.5\rho_0)$
$v_B \propto 2r^2\rho_0$

Taking the ratio of their terminal velocities:

$\dfrac{v_A}{v_B} = \dfrac{3r^2\rho_0}{2r^2\rho_0} = \dfrac{3}{2}$

Therefore, the ratio $v_A : v_B$ is $3:2$.

Answer: $3:2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two steel spheres, A and B, are falling through the same viscous oil. The ratio of the radius of sphere A to that of sphere B is $2:3$. If the ratio of their instantaneous velocities is $3:4$, what is the ratio of the viscous drag forces acting on sphere A and sphere B?
questions.solution:
According to Stokes' law, the viscous drag force $F_v$ on a sphere of radius $r$ moving with velocity $v$ in a fluid of viscosity $\eta$ is given by:

$F_v = 6\pi\eta r v$

Since both spheres are falling through the same oil, $\eta$ is constant. Therefore, the viscous drag force is directly proportional to the product of radius and velocity:
$F_v \propto r v$

The ratio of the viscous drag forces is:
$\dfrac{F_A}{F_B} = \left(\dfrac{r_A}{r_B}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{v_A}{v_B}\right)$

Substituting the given ratios:
$\dfrac{F_A}{F_B} = \left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right) = \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Thus, the ratio of the viscous drag forces is $1:2$.

Squaring the ratio of the radii (confusing the drag force proportionality with terminal velocity proportionality) would incorrectly yield $1:3$.

Answer: $1:2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An air bubble of radius $2 \text{ mm}$ is rising at a steady speed of $2.5 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$ through a liquid column. If the coefficient of viscosity of the liquid is $0.5 \text{ kg m}^{-1} \text{ s}^{-1}$, what is the magnitude and direction of the viscous drag force acting on the bubble?
questions.solution:
Given:
Radius of the bubble, $r = 2 \text{ mm} = 2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$
Steady velocity, $v = 2.5 \text{ cm s}^{-1} = 2.5 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m s}^{-1}$
Coefficient of viscosity, $\eta = 0.5 \text{ kg m}^{-1} \text{ s}^{-1}$

According to Stokes' law, the magnitude of the viscous drag force is:
$F = 6\pi\eta r v$
$F = 6\pi \times 0.5 \times (2 \times 10^{-3}) \times (2.5 \times 10^{-2})$
$F = 3\pi \times 5 \times 10^{-5}$
$F = 15\pi \times 10^{-5} \text{ N} = 1.5\pi \times 10^{-4} \text{ N}$

Viscous drag always opposes the relative motion of the object through the fluid. Since the air bubble is rising (moving vertically upwards), the viscous drag force must act vertically downwards.

Answer: $1.5\pi \times 10^{-4} \text{ N}$, vertically downwards

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An experiment is conducted to measure the pressure drop $\Delta P$ across a fixed horizontal constriction in a pipe for various steady volume flow rates $Q$ of an ideal fluid. Which of the following graphs best represents the variation of $\Delta P$ (on the y-axis) with $Q$ (on the x-axis)?
options: A straight line passing through the origin
A rectangular hyperbola in the first quadrant
A parabola opening towards the positive $Q$-axis
A parabola opening towards the positive $\Delta P$-axis
questions.solution:
Let the cross-sectional area of the wider part of the pipe be $A_1$ and that of the constriction be $A_2$.

From the equation of continuity, the volume flow rate is $Q = A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$.

The velocities at the two sections are $v_1 = \dfrac{Q}{A_1}$ and $v_2 = \dfrac{Q}{A_2}$.

Applying Bernoulli's principle for a horizontal pipe:

$P_1 + \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v_1^2 = P_2 + \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v_2^2$

The pressure drop $\Delta P$ is given by:

$\Delta P = P_1 - P_2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \rho (v_2^2 - v_1^2)$

Substituting the expressions for velocities:

$\Delta P = \dfrac{1}{2} \rho \left[ \left(\dfrac{Q}{A_2}\right)^2 - \left(\dfrac{Q}{A_1}\right)^2 \right]$

$\Delta P = \left[ \dfrac{1}{2} \rho \left( \dfrac{1}{A_2^2} - \dfrac{1}{A_1^2} \right) \right] Q^2$

Since the density $\rho$ and the areas $A_1$ and $A_2$ are constant for a given setup, the term in the square brackets is a positive constant $k$.

Thus, $\Delta P = k Q^2$.

This equation is of the form $y = k x^2$, which represents a parabola opening towards the positive y-axis (the $\Delta P$-axis).

Answer: A parabola opening towards the positive $\Delta P$-axis

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thin circular ring of radius $5\text{ cm}$ is placed gently on the surface of water. If the surface tension of water is $0.07\text{ N m}^{-1}$, the excess force required to lift the ring from the surface is (Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution:
For a thin circular ring, both the inner and outer boundaries are in contact with the liquid surface.

Total effective length of contact, $L = 2\pi R + 2\pi R = 4\pi R$

Excess force required, $F = T \times L = T \times 4\pi R$

$F = 0.07 \times 4 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 0.05$

$F = 0.01 \times 4 \times 22 \times 0.05 = 0.044\text{ N}$

$F = 44\text{ mN}$

Answer: $44\text{ mN}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An air bubble of radius $R$ is rising in a liquid of density $\rho$ and viscosity $\eta$. A solid spherical ball of the same radius $R$ and density $3\rho$ is falling in the same liquid. Neglecting the density of air, what is the ratio of the terminal speed of the air bubble to that of the solid ball?
questions.solution:
The terminal velocity $v$ of a spherical object of radius $r$ and density $\sigma$ moving in a liquid of density $\rho$ and viscosity $\eta$ is given by:

$v = \dfrac{2r^2g}{9\eta}|\sigma - \rho|$

For the rising air bubble, the density of air is negligible ($\sigma \approx 0$). The effective density difference driving the motion is $|0 - \rho| = \rho$.
Thus, its terminal speed is:
$v_1 = \dfrac{2R^2g\rho}{9\eta}$

For the falling solid ball, its density is $\sigma = 3\rho$. The effective density difference is $|3\rho - \rho| = 2\rho$.
Thus, its terminal speed is:
$v_2 = \dfrac{2R^2g(2\rho)}{9\eta}$

The ratio of their terminal speeds is:
$\dfrac{v_1}{v_2} = \dfrac{\rho}{2\rho} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Therefore, the ratio is $1 : 2$.

Answer: $1 : 2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For a solid sphere of a given material falling through a viscous liquid, the viscous force acting on it at terminal velocity is directly proportional to the cube of its radius.

Reason (R): The terminal velocity of a solid sphere falling through a viscous liquid is directly proportional to the cube of its radius.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
At terminal velocity, the net force on the sphere is zero. The downward weight is balanced by the upward buoyant force and viscous force.

$F_v = W - F_b$

$F_v = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho g - \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \sigma g$

$F_v = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 (\rho - \sigma) g$

Thus, the viscous force at terminal velocity is directly proportional to $r^3$. Therefore, Assertion (A) is true.

According to Stokes' law, the terminal velocity $v_t$ of a sphere is given by:

$v_t = \dfrac{2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9\eta}$

This shows that terminal velocity is directly proportional to the square of the radius ($r^2$), not the cube. Therefore, Reason (R) is false.

Answer: (A) is true but (R) is false

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The pressure exerted by water at the bottom of a conical flask and a cylindrical flask of the same base area and height is identical, even though they contain different amounts of water.
Reason (R): The hydrostatic pressure at a point inside a liquid at rest depends only on the depth of the point below the free surface and the density of the liquid, independent of the shape of the container.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true
questions.solution:
The hydrostatic pressure at a depth $h$ in a liquid of density $\rho$ is given by $P = \rho g h$.

This pressure depends only on the depth $h$ from the free surface, the density of the liquid $\rho$, and the acceleration due to gravity $g$. It does not depend on the shape of the container or the total volume of liquid present. This phenomenon is known as the hydrostatic paradox.

Since both the conical flask and the cylindrical flask are filled with water to the same height, the pressure at their bottoms will be identical, making Assertion (A) true.

Reason (R) correctly states the principle that pressure is independent of the container's shape and depends only on depth and density, which is the exact explanation for the phenomenon described in the assertion. Therefore, both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid sphere of volume $V$ and density $\rho$ is falling through a liquid of density $\sigma$. If the sphere has attained terminal velocity, what is the magnitude of the viscous drag force acting on it in terms of the given parameters? (where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution:
When the sphere attains terminal velocity, it moves with a constant velocity, meaning the net force acting on it is zero.

The forces acting on the sphere are:
1. Downward weight, $W = V\rho g$
2. Upward buoyant force, $F_B = V\sigma g$
3. Upward viscous drag force, $F_v$

For equilibrium at terminal velocity:
$W = F_B + F_v$

Rearranging for the viscous drag force:
$F_v = W - F_B$
$F_v = V\rho g - V\sigma g = V(\rho - \sigma)g$

Answer: $V(\rho - \sigma)g$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A student observes that the absolute pressure inside a soap bubble of radius $2.0\text{ mm}$ in the atmosphere is exactly equal to the absolute pressure at a depth of $1.6\text{ cm}$ inside an oil tank. If the density of the oil is $800\text{ kg m}^{-3}$ and the acceleration due to gravity is $10\text{ m s}^{-2}$, what is the surface tension of the soap solution?
questions.solution:
The absolute pressure inside a soap bubble of radius $R$ and surface tension $T$ is given by:
$P_{\text{bubble}} = P_0 + \dfrac{4T}{R}$

The absolute pressure at a depth $h$ in a liquid of density $\rho$ is:
$P_{\text{depth}} = P_0 + \rho g h$

Equating the two pressures:
$P_0 + \dfrac{4T}{R} = P_0 + \rho g h$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{4T}{R} = \rho g h$
$\Rightarrow T = \dfrac{\rho g h R}{4}$

Given values:
$R = 2.0\text{ mm} = 2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}$
$h = 1.6\text{ cm} = 1.6 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$
$\rho = 800\text{ kg m}^{-3}$
$g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$

Substituting the values:
$T = \dfrac{800 \times 10 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-2} \times 2 \times 10^{-3}}{4}$
$T = \dfrac{128 \times 2 \times 10^{-3}}{4}$
$T = 64 \times 10^{-3}\text{ N m}^{-1} = 0.064\text{ N m}^{-1}$

Answer: $0.064\text{ N m}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A scuba diver is exploring a freshwater lake at a depth of $10$ m. What is the ratio of the absolute pressure to the gauge pressure experienced by the diver at this depth?
(Take the density of water as $1000$ kg m$^{-3}$, atmospheric pressure as $1 \times 10^5$ Pa, and $g = 10$ m/s$^2$)
questions.solution:
The gauge pressure at a depth $h$ is given by $P_{\text{gauge}} = \rho g h$.

Given:
$h = 10$ m
$\rho = 1000$ kg m$^{-3}$
$g = 10$ m/s$^2$

Substituting the values:
$P_{\text{gauge}} = 1000 \times 10 \times 10 = 1 \times 10^5$ Pa

The absolute pressure is the sum of atmospheric pressure and gauge pressure:
$P_{\text{abs}} = P_{\text{atm}} + P_{\text{gauge}}$

Given $P_{\text{atm}} = 1 \times 10^5$ Pa:
$P_{\text{abs}} = 1 \times 10^5 + 1 \times 10^5 = 2 \times 10^5$ Pa

The required ratio is:
$\dfrac{P_{\text{abs}}}{P_{\text{gauge}}} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^5}{1 \times 10^5} = \dfrac{2}{1}$

The ratio is $2:1$.

Answer: $2:1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small spherical ball of radius $r$ falls from rest in a long column of a viscous liquid. After it reaches terminal velocity, the rate of heat production due to viscous friction is proportional to $r^n$. The value of $n$ is:
questions.solution:
The rate of heat production is equal to the mechanical power dissipated by the viscous drag force.

Power $P = F \times v$, where $F$ is the viscous drag force and $v$ is the terminal velocity.

According to Stokes' law, the viscous drag force at terminal velocity is $F = 6\pi\eta r v$.

Therefore, the rate of heat production is:

$P = (6\pi\eta r v) \times v = 6\pi\eta r v^2$

The terminal velocity $v$ of a spherical ball of radius $r$ is given by:

$v = \dfrac{2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9\eta}$

This shows that $v \propto r^2$.

Substituting $v \propto r^2$ into the power equation:

$P \propto r \times (r^2)^2$

$P \propto r \times r^4 = r^5$

Thus, the rate of heat production is proportional to $r^5$, which means $n = 5$.

Answer: $5$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The absolute pressure at a depth $h$ below the free surface of a liquid is not directly proportional to the depth $h$.
Reason (R): Absolute pressure is the sum of atmospheric pressure and gauge pressure, where the atmospheric pressure acts as a non-zero constant.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true
questions.solution:
The absolute pressure $P$ at a depth $h$ is given by $P = P_{atm} + \rho g h$.

For a quantity to be directly proportional to another, their relationship must be of the form $y = kx$ (a straight line passing through the origin).

Because of the presence of the atmospheric pressure term ($P_{atm}$), which is a non-zero constant, the relationship between $P$ and $h$ is linear but not directly proportional. The graph of $P$ versus $h$ has a positive y-intercept.

Therefore, the Assertion is true. The Reason correctly identifies that the absolute pressure includes this non-zero constant (atmospheric pressure) alongside the gauge pressure ($\rho g h$), which perfectly explains why the relationship is not a direct proportionality. Thus, the Reason is true and is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An air bubble of radius $R$ is formed at a depth $h$ in a liquid of density $\rho$ and surface tension $T$. The absolute pressure inside this air bubble is found to be equal to the absolute pressure inside a soap bubble of radius $2R$ situated in the open atmosphere. If the atmospheric pressure is $P_0$, what is the surface tension $T'$ of the soap solution?
questions.solution:
The absolute pressure inside an air bubble of radius $R$ at a depth $h$ in a liquid is the sum of atmospheric pressure, hydrostatic pressure, and the excess pressure (which has only one free surface):
$P_{\text{air bubble}} = P_0 + \rho g h + \dfrac{2T}{R}$

The absolute pressure inside a soap bubble of radius $2R$ in the atmosphere (which has two free surfaces) is:
$P_{\text{soap bubble}} = P_0 + \dfrac{4T'}{(2R)} = P_0 + \dfrac{2T'}{R}$

According to the problem, these two absolute pressures are equal:
$P_0 + \rho g h + \dfrac{2T}{R} = P_0 + \dfrac{2T'}{R}$

Cancelling $P_0$ from both sides:
$\rho g h + \dfrac{2T}{R} = \dfrac{2T'}{R}$

Multiplying the entire equation by $\dfrac{R}{2}$ to isolate $T'$:
$T' = \dfrac{\rho g h R}{2} + T$

Answer: $T + \dfrac{\rho g h R}{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Match List I with List II regarding the excess force required to detach various objects from a liquid surface of surface tension $T$.

List I (Object)List II (Excess force)
A. Circular disc of radius $r$I. $8aT$
B. Circular ring of radius $r$II. $4aT$
C. Square plate of side $a$III. $4\pi rT$
D. Square frame of side $a$IV. $2\pi rT$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
The excess force required to detach an object from a liquid surface is given by $F = T \times L_{\text{eff}}$, where $L_{\text{eff}}$ is the effective length of the boundary in contact with the liquid.

A. Circular disc of radius $r$: The liquid touches only the outer perimeter. $L_{\text{eff}} = 2\pi r$. Excess force = $2\pi rT$. (Matches IV)

B. Circular ring of radius $r$: The liquid touches both the inner and outer perimeters. $L_{\text{eff}} = 2\pi r + 2\pi r = 4\pi r$. Excess force = $4\pi rT$. (Matches III)

C. Square plate of side $a$: The liquid touches only the outer perimeter. $L_{\text{eff}} = 4a$. Excess force = $4aT$. (Matches II)

D. Square frame of side $a$: The liquid touches both the inner and outer perimeters. $L_{\text{eff}} = 4a + 4a = 8a$. Excess force = $8aT$. (Matches I)

Therefore, the correct matching is A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I.

Answer: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Water flows downwards through a vertical tapering pipe. The cross-sectional area of the top end is $4 \text{ cm}^2$ and that of the bottom end is $2 \text{ cm}^2$. The vertical distance between the two ends is $15 \text{ cm}$. If the pressure of water at the top end is equal to the pressure at the bottom end, what is the volume flow rate of water through the pipe?
(Take $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
Let the top end be section 1 and the bottom end be section 2.

Given:
$A_1 = 4 \text{ cm}^2$
$A_2 = 2 \text{ cm}^2$
$h = 15 \text{ cm}$
$g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2} = 1000 \text{ cm s}^{-2}$
$P_1 = P_2$

Applying Bernoulli's equation between the top and bottom ends:

$P_1 + \rho g h + \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v_1^2 = P_2 + 0 + \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v_2^2$

Since $P_1 = P_2$, the pressure terms cancel out:

$\rho g h + \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v_1^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v_2^2$

$2 g h = v_2^2 - v_1^2$

From the equation of continuity, the volume flow rate $Q = A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$.

Thus, $v_1 = \dfrac{Q}{4}$ and $v_2 = \dfrac{Q}{2}$.

Substitute these into the simplified Bernoulli's equation:

$2 \times 1000 \times 15 = \left(\dfrac{Q}{2}\right)^2 - \left(\dfrac{Q}{4}\right)^2$

$30000 = \dfrac{Q^2}{4} - \dfrac{Q^2}{16}$

$30000 = \dfrac{4Q^2 - Q^2}{16}$

$30000 = \dfrac{3Q^2}{16}$

$Q^2 = \dfrac{30000 \times 16}{3} = 10000 \times 16 = 160000$

$Q = \sqrt{160000} = 400 \text{ cm}^3 \text{ s}^{-1}$

Answer: $400 \text{ cm}^3 \text{ s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II for a small solid sphere of volume $V$, radius $r$ and density $\rho$ falling through a viscous fluid of density $\sigma$ (where $\rho \gt \sigma$) and coefficient of viscosity $\eta$.

List-IList-II
(A) Buoyant force(I) $V\sigma g$
(B) Initial acceleration when just released(II) $V(\rho - \sigma)g$
(C) Viscous force at terminal velocity(III) $g\left(1 - \dfrac{\sigma}{\rho}\right)$
(D) Terminal velocity(IV) $\dfrac{2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9\eta}$


Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
(A) Buoyant force is the weight of the displaced fluid. For a sphere of volume $V$ in a fluid of density $\sigma$, $F_b = V\sigma g$. This matches (I).

(B) When just released, the initial velocity is zero, so the viscous force is zero. The net downward force is $W - F_b = V\rho g - V\sigma g$.
Initial acceleration $a = \dfrac{\text{Net force}}{\text{Mass}} = \dfrac{V(\rho - \sigma)g}{V\rho} = g\left(1 - \dfrac{\sigma}{\rho}\right)$. This matches (III).

(C) At terminal velocity, the sphere moves with constant velocity, so the net force is zero.
Viscous force $F_v = W - F_b = V\rho g - V\sigma g = V(\rho - \sigma)g$. This matches (II).

(D) The terminal velocity of a sphere of radius $r$ falling in a viscous fluid of coefficient of viscosity $\eta$ is given by Stokes' law as $v_t = \dfrac{2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9\eta}$. This matches (IV).

Therefore, the correct matching is (A) - (I), (B) - (III), (C) - (II), (D) - (IV).

Answer: (A) - (I), (B) - (III), (C) - (II), (D) - (IV)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): As an air bubble rises from the bottom of a deep lake to the surface, the excess pressure of the air inside it relative to the surrounding water decreases.

Reason (R): The excess pressure inside an air bubble is directly proportional to the radius of the bubble.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is correct: As an air bubble rises, the depth of the water column above it decreases, which reduces the external hydrostatic pressure. According to Boyle's law, as the external pressure decreases, the volume of the air bubble increases, meaning its radius $R$ increases.

The excess pressure inside an air bubble in a liquid is given by $\Delta P = \dfrac{2T}{R}$. Since the radius $R$ increases as the bubble rises, the excess pressure $\Delta P$ must decrease.

Reason (R) is incorrect: The formula $\Delta P = \dfrac{2T}{R}$ shows that the excess pressure is inversely proportional to the radius of the bubble, not directly proportional.

Therefore, (A) is correct but (R) is not correct.

Answer: (A) is correct but (R) is not correct

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When a mercury barometer tube is tilted by an angle $\theta$ from the vertical, the length of the mercury column inside the tube increases.
Reason (R): The vertical height of the mercury column remains constant as it depends only on the external atmospheric pressure and the density of mercury.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution:
The atmospheric pressure supports a vertical column of mercury of height $h$, given by $P = \rho g h$.

Since the atmospheric pressure $P$ and the density of mercury $\rho$ are constant, the vertical height $h$ of the mercury column must remain constant, regardless of the tilt of the tube. Thus, the Reason is true.

When the tube is tilted by an angle $\theta$ from the vertical, the length of the mercury column $l$ along the tube is related to the vertical height $h$ by $h = l \cos\theta$.

Therefore, $l = \dfrac{h}{\cos\theta}$. Since $\cos\theta \lt 1$ for any tilt angle $\theta \gt 0$, the length $l$ must be greater than $h$. Thus, the length of the mercury column increases. The Assertion is true.

The constant vertical height is the exact geometric reason why the length along the tilted tube must increase. Hence, the Reason perfectly explains the Assertion.

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small glass marble falls through a column of liquid having a viscosity of $0.2 \text{ Pa s}$. If the instantaneous velocity of the marble is $0.5 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the viscous drag force acting on it is $6\pi \times 10^{-4} \text{ N}$, what is the diameter of the marble?
questions.solution:
According to Stokes' law, the viscous drag force acting on a spherical body is given by:

$F_v = 6\pi\eta r v$

Substituting the given values:
$6\pi \times 10^{-4} = 6\pi \times 0.2 \times r \times 0.5$

Cancelling $6\pi$ from both sides:
$10^{-4} = 0.1 \times r$

$r = \dfrac{10^{-4}}{0.1} = 10^{-3} \text{ m} = 1 \text{ mm}$

The diameter of the marble is:
$d = 2r = 2 \times 1 \text{ mm} = 2 \text{ mm}$

Stopping at the radius leads to the incorrect answer of $1 \text{ mm}$.

Answer: $2 \text{ mm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two solid spheres, A and B, are made of the same material and are allowed to fall through a large column of a viscous liquid. The ratio of the radius of sphere A to that of sphere B is $1:2$. When both spheres have attained their respective terminal velocities, the ratio of the viscous drag force on sphere A to that on sphere B is:
questions.solution:
According to Stokes' law, the viscous drag force on a spherical body is:
$\mathrm{F} = 6 \pi \eta r v$

The terminal velocity $v_t$ of a sphere falling through a viscous fluid is given by:
$v_t = \dfrac{2}{9} \dfrac{r^2 (\rho - \sigma) g}{\eta}$

This shows that the terminal velocity is directly proportional to the square of the radius ($v_t \propto r^2$).

Substituting $v_t$ into the drag force equation gives:
$\mathrm{F} \propto r \times r^2$
$\mathrm{F} \propto r^3$

Alternatively, at terminal velocity, the net force is zero, meaning the viscous drag force balances the effective weight (weight minus buoyant force). Since effective weight is proportional to the volume of the sphere, $\mathrm{F} \propto r^3$.

Given the ratio of radii $r_A : r_B = 1:2$, the ratio of the viscous drag forces is:
$\dfrac{\mathrm{F}_A}{\mathrm{F}_B} = \left(\dfrac{r_A}{r_B}\right)^3 = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \dfrac{1}{8}$

Answer: $1:8$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Which of the following devices or phenomena does NOT work on the basis of Bernoulli's principle?
questions.solution:
Venturi-meter, atomiser, and the dynamic lift of an aeroplane are all direct applications of Bernoulli's principle, as they rely on the relationship between fluid speed and pressure.

A hydraulic lift works on the basis of Pascal's law, which states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every portion of the fluid and the walls of the containing vessel.

Answer: Hydraulic lift

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When an incompressible ideal fluid flows steadily through a horizontal pipe of varying cross-section, the fluid velocity is maximum at the narrowest part of the pipe.
Reason (R): According to Bernoulli's principle, for a steady horizontal flow of an ideal fluid, a region of higher fluid velocity is accompanied by a lower static pressure.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true: According to the equation of continuity for an incompressible fluid, $A_1v_1 = A_2v_2$. The velocity of the fluid is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area. Therefore, the fluid velocity is maximum at the narrowest part of the pipe where the area is minimum.

Reason (R) is true: Bernoulli's principle for a horizontal pipe states that $P + \dfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2 = \text{constant}$. This implies that an increase in fluid velocity results in a decrease in static pressure.

However, Reason (R) is not the correct explanation for Assertion (A). The maximum velocity at the narrowest part is a direct consequence of the conservation of mass (equation of continuity), not the conservation of energy (Bernoulli's principle). Therefore, both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) does not explain (A).

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small glass marble of radius $2 \mathrm{~mm}$ falls with a constant velocity of $5 \mathrm{~cm} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ through a tall cylinder filled with a liquid. If the viscous drag force acting on the marble is $3.768 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~N}$, the coefficient of viscosity of the liquid is: (Take $\pi = 3.14$)
questions.solution:
According to Stokes' law, the viscous drag force is given by:
$\mathrm{F} = 6 \pi \eta r v$

Rearranging the formula to solve for the coefficient of viscosity $\eta$:
$\eta = \dfrac{\mathrm{F}}{6 \pi r v}$

Given values:
$\mathrm{F} = 3.768 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~N}$
$r = 2 \mathrm{~mm} = 2 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}$
$v = 5 \mathrm{~cm} \mathrm{~s}^{-1} = 5 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$

Substituting the values:
$\eta = \dfrac{3.768 \times 10^{-3}}{6 \times 3.14 \times 2 \times 10^{-3} \times 5 \times 10^{-2}}$

$\eta = \dfrac{3.768 \times 10^{-3}}{18.84 \times 10 \times 10^{-5}}$

$\eta = \dfrac{3.768 \times 10^{-3}}{1.884 \times 10^{-3}}$

$\eta = 2.0 \mathrm{~Pa}\cdot\mathrm{s}$

Answer: $2.0 \mathrm{~Pa}\cdot\mathrm{s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In a horizontal venturi-meter, the fluid pressure is minimum at the narrowest cross-section (throat).
Reason (R): According to the equation of continuity, fluid velocity is maximum at the narrowest cross-section, and by Bernoulli's principle, an increase in velocity is accompanied by a decrease in pressure.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
For an incompressible fluid flowing through a horizontal pipe, the equation of continuity states that $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$. At the narrowest cross-section (throat), the area $A$ is minimum, so the fluid velocity $v$ is maximum.

According to Bernoulli's principle for a horizontal flow, $P + \dfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2 = \text{constant}$.

Since the velocity is maximum at the throat, the pressure $P$ must be minimum to keep the sum constant. Therefore, both Assertion and Reason are correct, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion.

Answer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three vessels $A$, $B$, and $C$ have identical base areas. Vessel $A$ is cylindrical, vessel $B$ is wider at the top, and vessel $C$ is wider at the base. All three vessels are filled with the same liquid up to the exact same height $h$. If $F_A$, $F_B$, and $F_C$ are the forces exerted by the liquid on the base of vessels $A$, $B$, and $C$ respectively, which of the following relations is correct?
questions.solution:
The pressure $P$ exerted by a liquid at a depth $h$ is given by $P = \rho g h$.

Since all three vessels are filled with the same liquid to the same height $h$, the pressure at the base of each vessel is identical.

The force exerted by the liquid on the base is given by $F = P \times A$, where $A$ is the base area.

As the base areas of all three vessels are identical, the force exerted by the liquid on the base is exactly the same for all three vessels, regardless of their shapes or the total volume of liquid they contain. Thus, $F_A = F_B = F_C$.

Answer: $F_A = F_B = F_C$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A venturi-meter is used to measure the volume flow rate of an ideal liquid flowing through a pipe. If the pressure difference between the broader section and the narrow throat of the venturi-meter is doubled, by what factor does the volume flow rate of the liquid change?
questions.solution:
The volume flow rate $Q$ through a venturi-meter is given by the formula derived from Bernoulli's principle and the equation of continuity:

$Q = A a \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \Delta P}{\rho (A^2 - a^2)}}$

where $A$ and $a$ are the cross-sectional areas of the broader section and the throat respectively, $\rho$ is the density of the liquid, and $\Delta P$ is the pressure difference between the two sections.

From the formula, it is clear that the volume flow rate is directly proportional to the square root of the pressure difference, i.e., $Q \propto \sqrt{\Delta P}$.

If the pressure difference $\Delta P$ is doubled, the new flow rate $Q'$ will be proportional to $\sqrt{2 \Delta P}$.

Therefore, $Q' = \sqrt{2} Q$, meaning the volume flow rate increases by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$.

Answer: Increases by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A U-tube contains water and an unknown immiscible liquid in equilibrium. The height of the water column is $20\text{ cm}$ and the height of the unknown liquid column is $25\text{ cm}$ above the common interface level. If the density of water is $1000\text{ kg m}^{-3}$, what is the density of the unknown liquid?
questions.solution:
At the common interface level, the hydrostatic pressure exerted by both liquid columns must be equal.

$P_{\text{water}} = P_{\text{liquid}}$

$\rho_{\text{water}} g h_{\text{water}} = \rho_{\text{liquid}} g h_{\text{liquid}}$

$1000 \times 20 = \rho_{\text{liquid}} \times 25$

$\rho_{\text{liquid}} = \dfrac{1000 \times 20}{25} = 800\text{ kg m}^{-3}$

Answer: $800\text{ kg m}^{-3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When two solid spheres of the same material but radii $r$ and $2r$ fall in a viscous liquid, the viscous drag force on the larger sphere at terminal velocity is 8 times that on the smaller sphere.

Reason (R): The viscous drag force on a sphere at terminal velocity is directly proportional to the cube of its radius.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is correct but Reason (R) is not correct
Assertion (A) is not correct but Reason (R) is correct
questions.solution:
At terminal velocity, the net force on the falling sphere is zero. The viscous drag force ($F_v$) exactly balances the effective weight of the sphere (actual weight minus buoyant force).

$F_v = W - F_B$
$F_v = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \sigma g - \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho g$
$F_v = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 (\sigma - \rho) g$

For a given material (constant $\sigma$) and liquid (constant $\rho$), the viscous drag force at terminal velocity is directly proportional to the volume of the sphere, and hence to the cube of its radius ($F_v \propto r^3$).

Therefore, Reason (R) is correct.

Using this proportionality for spheres of radii $r$ and $2r$:
$\dfrac{F_{v2}}{F_{v1}} = \left(\dfrac{2r}{r}\right)^3 = 8$

The drag force on the larger sphere is 8 times that on the smaller sphere. Thus, Assertion (A) is correct.

Since Reason (R) provides the exact mathematical relationship used to derive Assertion (A), it is the correct explanation.

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A tank contains three immiscible liquids stacked on top of each other. The layers consist of water (density $1\text{ g cm}^{-3}$), an oil (density $0.8\text{ g cm}^{-3}$), and mercury (density $13.6\text{ g cm}^{-3}$), each having a column height of $10\text{ cm}$. What is the height of a pure water column that would exert the exact same hydrostatic pressure at the bottom of the tank?
questions.solution:
The total hydrostatic pressure at the bottom of the tank is the sum of the pressures exerted by each liquid layer.

$P_{\text{total}} = \rho_{\text{water}} g h + \rho_{\text{oil}} g h + \rho_{\text{mercury}} g h$

$P_{\text{total}} = (1 + 0.8 + 13.6) \times g \times 10$

$P_{\text{total}} = 15.4 \times 10 \times g = 154 g$

For an equivalent pure water column of height $H_{\text{equiv}}$:

$P_{\text{water}} = \rho_{\text{water}} g H_{\text{equiv}} = 1 \times g \times H_{\text{equiv}}$

Equating the pressures:

$1 \times g \times H_{\text{equiv}} = 154 g$

$H_{\text{equiv}} = 154\text{ cm}$

Answer: $154\text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Read the following statements carefully:

Statement I: The force exerted by a liquid on the base of a container is always equal to the total weight of the liquid in the container.
Statement II: In interconnected vessels of different shapes, a liquid at rest will reach the same horizontal level in all vessels.
Statement III: The hydrostatic pressure at a depth $h$ in a liquid is independent of the cross-sectional area of the containing vessel.
Statement IV: If a vessel is wider at the top than at the base, the force exerted by the liquid on its base is greater than the weight of the liquid it contains.

How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.solution:
Let us evaluate each statement individually:

Statement I is incorrect. Due to the hydrostatic paradox, the force exerted by a liquid on the base of a container ($F = P \times A = \rho g h A$) is not necessarily equal to the total weight of the liquid. It is only equal if the vessel is perfectly cylindrical or prismatic.

Statement II is correct. In interconnected vessels, the liquid reaches the same horizontal level to ensure the pressure is equal at all points on the same horizontal plane, regardless of the shapes of the individual vessels.

Statement III is correct. The hydrostatic pressure at a depth $h$ is given by $P = \rho g h$, which depends only on depth and density, not on the cross-sectional area.

Statement IV is incorrect. For a vessel wider at the top than at the base, the actual volume of the liquid $V$ is greater than the volume of a cylinder with the same base area and height ($V \gt A \times h$). Thus, the weight of the liquid ($W = \rho V g$) is greater than the force on the base ($F = \rho A h g$). The statement incorrectly claims the force is greater than the weight.

Therefore, exactly two statements (II and III) are correct.

Answer: Two

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal fluid of density $\rho$ flows steadily through a horizontal pipe. The pipe narrows from a radius of $2r$ at section 1 to a radius of $r$ at section 2. If the velocity of the fluid at section 1 is $v$, the pressure difference between section 1 and section 2 ($P_1 - P_2$) is:
questions.solution:
According to the equation of continuity, $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$.
Given $r_1 = 2r$ and $r_2 = r$, the areas are $A_1 = \pi (2r)^2 = 4\pi r^2$ and $A_2 = \pi r^2$.
Substituting the values:
$(4\pi r^2) v = (\pi r^2) v_2 \Rightarrow v_2 = 4v$

Applying Bernoulli's principle for a horizontal pipe ($h_1 = h_2$):
$P_1 + \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v_1^2 = P_2 + \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v_2^2$

Substituting $v_1 = v$ and $v_2 = 4v$:
$P_1 + \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v^2 = P_2 + \dfrac{1}{2} \rho (4v)^2$
$P_1 - P_2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \rho (16v^2) - \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v^2$
$P_1 - P_2 = \dfrac{15}{2} \rho v^2$

Answer: $\dfrac{15}{2} \rho v^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The variation of gauge pressure ($P$) with depth ($h$) for two different liquids A and B is plotted on a graph. The straight line for liquid A makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with the $h$-axis, while the line for liquid B makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the $h$-axis. What is the ratio of the density of liquid A to that of liquid B?
questions.solution:
Gauge pressure at a depth $h$ in a liquid of density $\rho$ is given by $P = \rho gh$.

Rearranging this equation, we get $\dfrac{P}{h} = \rho g$.

On a graph of $P$ (y-axis) versus $h$ (x-axis), the slope of the line is equal to $\dfrac{P}{h}$. Therefore, the slope is directly proportional to the density of the liquid ($\text{Slope} = \rho g$).

For liquid A, the slope is $\tan(60^\circ) = \sqrt{3}$.

For liquid B, the slope is $\tan(30^\circ) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.

The ratio of their densities is:
$\dfrac{\rho_A}{\rho_B} = \dfrac{\text{Slope}_A}{\text{Slope}_B} = \dfrac{\tan(60^\circ)}{\tan(30^\circ)} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}} = 3$

Thus, the ratio of the density of liquid A to liquid B is $3:1$.

Answer: $3:1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The variation of absolute pressure $P$ with depth $h$ below the free surface of an unknown liquid is plotted on a graph. The graph is a straight line that gives $P = 1 \times 10^5$ Pa at $h = 0$ m, and $P = 2.2 \times 10^5$ Pa at $h = 10$ m. Assuming the acceleration due to gravity $g = 10$ m/s$^2$, what is the density of the liquid?
questions.solution:
The absolute pressure $P$ at a depth $h$ is given by the equation:
$P = P_{atm} + \rho g h$

This represents a linear equation of the form $y = c + mx$, where the slope of the $P$ versus $h$ graph is $m = \rho g$.

From the given data, the slope is:
$\dfrac{\Delta P}{\Delta h} = \dfrac{2.2 \times 10^5 - 1 \times 10^5}{10 - 0}$
$\dfrac{\Delta P}{\Delta h} = \dfrac{1.2 \times 10^5}{10} = 1.2 \times 10^4$ Pa/m

Equating this slope to $\rho g$:
$\rho g = 1.2 \times 10^4$
$\rho \times 10 = 12000$
$\rho = 1200$ kg/m$^3$

Using $P/h$ at $h=10$ without subtracting the intercept leads to the incorrect $2200$ kg/m$^3$.

Answer: $1200$ kg/m$^3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Two spheres of the same material and radii $R$ and $2R$ fall through the same viscous liquid. When they attain their respective terminal velocities, the ratio of the viscous drag forces on them is $1 : 8$.

Reason (R): The viscous drag force on a sphere moving at its terminal velocity is directly proportional to the cube of its radius.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
According to Stokes' law, the viscous drag force is given by $F_v = 6\pi\eta r v$.

The terminal velocity $v_t$ of a sphere of radius $r$ and density $\rho$ falling in a liquid of density $\sigma$ and viscosity $\eta$ is given by $v_t = \dfrac{2}{9}\dfrac{r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{\eta}$.

Therefore, the terminal velocity is directly proportional to the square of the radius ($v_t \propto r^2$).

Substituting this into Stokes' law, we get $F_v \propto r(r^2) \Rightarrow F_v \propto r^3$.

Thus, the Reason is correct.

For two spheres of radii $R$ and $2R$, the ratio of their viscous drag forces at terminal velocity will be $R^3 : (2R)^3 = 1 : 8$.

Thus, the Assertion is also correct, and the Reason is the correct explanation for the Assertion.

Answer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two spherical raindrops of masses $m$ and $8m$ fall through the air. Assuming the density of the raindrops is uniform and neglecting the buoyant force of air, the ratio of their terminal velocities is:
questions.solution:
Let the radii of the two raindrops be $r_1$ and $r_2$.

Since the density $\rho$ is the same for both raindrops, mass $m = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho$.

Therefore, $m \propto r^3$.

Given the ratio of masses is $m : 8m = 1 : 8$, the ratio of their radii is:

$\dfrac{r_1}{r_2} = \left( \dfrac{1}{8} \right)^{\dfrac{1}{3}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

The terminal velocity $v$ of a spherical drop falling through a viscous medium is given by Stokes' law:

$v = \dfrac{2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9\eta}$

Thus, terminal velocity $v \propto r^2$.

The ratio of their terminal velocities is:

$\dfrac{v_1}{v_2} = \left( \dfrac{r_1}{r_2} \right)^2 = \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{4}$

Hence, the ratio is $1 : 4$.

Answer: $1 : 4$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When two solid spheres of the same material but different radii are dropped from rest into a long column of a given viscous liquid, they will have the same initial acceleration.

Reason (R): The terminal velocity of a sphere falling through a viscous medium is independent of its radius.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is correct. The initial acceleration of a sphere dropped in a viscous liquid is determined by the net force at $t=0$, where velocity and viscous drag are zero. The acceleration is $a = \dfrac{mg - F_b}{m} = g\left(1 - \dfrac{\sigma}{\rho}\right)$, where $\rho$ is the density of the material and $\sigma$ is the density of the liquid. This expression is independent of the radius of the sphere.

Reason (R) is incorrect. According to Stokes' law, the terminal velocity is given by $v_t = \dfrac{2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9\eta}$. Thus, terminal velocity is directly proportional to the square of the radius ($v_t \propto r^2$) and is not independent of it.

Answer: (A) is correct but (R) is not correct

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An incompressible, ideal fluid flows steadily through a horizontal pipe of varying circular cross-section. A graph is plotted between the kinetic energy per unit volume ($K$) of the fluid on the y-axis and the radius ($r$) of the pipe on the x-axis. Which of the following best describes the shape of this graph?
options: A straight line with a negative slope
questions.solution:
For the steady flow of an incompressible fluid, the volume flow rate $Q$ is constant.

According to the equation of continuity:
$Q = A v = \pi r^2 v$
$\Rightarrow v = \dfrac{Q}{\pi r^2}$

The kinetic energy per unit volume ($K$) is given by:
$K = \dfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2$

Substituting the expression for $v$:
$K = \dfrac{1}{2}\rho \left(\dfrac{Q}{\pi r^2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{\rho Q^2}{2\pi^2 r^4}$

Since $\rho$ and $Q$ are constants for a given steady flow, we get:
$K \propto \dfrac{1}{r^4}$ or $K \propto r^{-4}$

Thus, the graph between $K$ and $r$ will be a non-linear curve representing an inverse fourth-power relationship.

Answer: A non-linear curve representing $K \propto r^{-4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small metallic sphere of mass $m$ and density $\rho$ is dropped into a tall cylinder containing a viscous liquid. Once the sphere reaches terminal velocity, the viscous force acting on it is observed to be exactly one-fourth of its weight. What is the density of the viscous liquid?
questions.solution:
When the sphere reaches terminal velocity, the net force acting on it is zero. This means the downward weight ($W$) is balanced by the sum of the upward buoyant force ($F_b$) and the viscous force ($F_v$).

$W = F_b + F_v$

Given that the viscous force is one-fourth of the weight ($F_v = \dfrac{mg}{4}$):

$mg = F_b + \dfrac{mg}{4}$

$F_b = mg - \dfrac{mg}{4} = \dfrac{3mg}{4}$

The buoyant force is also given by the weight of the displaced liquid: $F_b = V \sigma g$, where $V$ is the volume of the sphere and $\sigma$ is the density of the liquid.

The volume of the sphere can be written as $V = \dfrac{m}{\rho}$. Substituting this into the buoyant force equation:

$\left(\dfrac{m}{\rho}\right) \sigma g = \dfrac{3mg}{4}$

$\dfrac{\sigma}{\rho} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

$\sigma = \dfrac{3\rho}{4}$

Answer: $\dfrac{3\rho}{4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A spherical ball is dropped from rest into a long column of a highly viscous liquid. Which of the following descriptions best represents the variation of the magnitude of the ball's acceleration ($a$) as a function of time ($t$)?
options: A horizontal straight line parallel to the time axis.
A straight line starting from a positive maximum value on the acceleration axis and decreasing linearly to zero.
A curve starting from the origin and increasing asymptotically to a constant positive value.
A curve starting from a positive maximum value on the acceleration axis and decreasing asymptotically to zero.
questions.solution:
When the ball is dropped from rest, its initial velocity is zero. The viscous drag force is initially zero. The initial acceleration is at its maximum, determined by the effective weight (gravity minus buoyancy).

As the ball falls and gains velocity, the upward viscous drag force ($F_v = 6\pi\eta r v$) increases. The net downward force decreases, which means the acceleration decreases.

According to Newton's second law, $ma = W_{eff} - F_v$. Thus, $a = a_0 - \dfrac{6\pi\eta r}{m} v$.

Since velocity increases and approaches a constant terminal velocity asymptotically, the acceleration decreases and asymptotically approaches zero. Therefore, the acceleration-time graph is a curve starting from a positive maximum value on the y-axis and decreasing asymptotically to zero on the x-axis.

Answer: A curve starting from a positive maximum value on the acceleration axis and decreasing asymptotically to zero.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The gauge pressure inside a soap bubble of surface tension $T$ is equal to the pressure exerted by a liquid column of density $\rho$ and height $h$. What is the work done in blowing this soap bubble from zero radius? (Let $g$ be the acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution:
Excess pressure inside a soap bubble is given by $\Delta P = \dfrac{4T}{R}$, where $R$ is the radius of the bubble.

Gauge pressure exerted by a liquid column of height $h$ and density $\rho$ is $P = \rho g h$.

Equating the two pressures as given:
$\dfrac{4T}{R} = \rho g h \implies R = \dfrac{4T}{\rho g h}$

The work done in blowing a soap bubble from zero radius is equal to its surface energy. Since a soap bubble has two free surfaces (inner and outer), the work done is:
$W = T \times 2 \times 4\pi R^2 = 8\pi R^2 T$

Substituting the value of $R$ into the work equation:
$W = 8\pi T \left(\dfrac{4T}{\rho g h}\right)^2$

$W = 8\pi T \left(\dfrac{16T^2}{\rho^2 g^2 h^2}\right) = \dfrac{128\pi T^3}{\rho^2 g^2 h^2}$

Note: Using $W = 4\pi R^2 T$ (forgetting the two surfaces for work) leads to the incorrect option $\dfrac{64\pi T^3}{\rho^2 g^2 h^2}$, and using $\Delta P = \dfrac{2T}{R}$ (forgetting two surfaces for pressure) leads to the incorrect option $\dfrac{32\pi T^3}{\rho^2 g^2 h^2}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small metal sphere is dropped from rest into a long column of a viscous liquid at $20^\circ\text{C}$. It attains a terminal velocity $v_1$, and its initial acceleration at the moment of release is $a_1$. The same liquid is then heated to $60^\circ\text{C}$, which significantly reduces its viscosity. The experiment is repeated with the same sphere, which now attains a terminal velocity $v_2$ and has an initial acceleration $a_2$. Assuming the densities of the metal and the liquid do not change significantly with temperature, which of the following relations is correct?
questions.solution:
The terminal velocity of a sphere falling through a viscous liquid is given by $v_t = \dfrac{2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9\eta}$.

When the temperature of the liquid increases from $20^\circ\text{C}$ to $60^\circ\text{C}$, its viscosity $\eta$ decreases. Since $v_t$ is inversely proportional to $\eta$, the terminal velocity increases, meaning $v_2 \gt v_1$.

The initial acceleration of the sphere at the moment it is dropped ($v=0$) is determined only by gravity and the buoyant force. It is given by $a = g\left(1 - \dfrac{\sigma}{\rho}\right)$, where $\rho$ is the density of the sphere and $\sigma$ is the density of the liquid. Since the densities do not change significantly, the initial acceleration remains unchanged, meaning $a_1 = a_2$.

Answer: $v_2 \gt v_1$ and $a_1 = a_2$

questions.q: Oil of density $800 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$ flows steadily through a horizontal pipe. The cross-sectional areas of the pipe at two sections A and B are $40 \text{ cm}^2$ and $10 \text{ cm}^2$ respectively. If the volume flow rate of the oil is $2000 \text{ cm}^3 \text{ s}^{-1}$, what is the pressure difference between the two sections?
questions.solution:
From the given volume flow rate $Q$, the velocity of oil at section A is:

$v_A = \dfrac{Q}{A_A} = \dfrac{2000 \text{ cm}^3 \text{ s}^{-1}}{40 \text{ cm}^2} = 50 \text{ cm s}^{-1} = 0.5 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

The velocity at section B is:

$v_B = \dfrac{Q}{A_B} = \dfrac{2000 \text{ cm}^3 \text{ s}^{-1}}{10 \text{ cm}^2} = 200 \text{ cm s}^{-1} = 2 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

According to Bernoulli's principle for a horizontal pipe:

$P_A + \dfrac{1}{2}\rho v_A^2 = P_B + \dfrac{1}{2}\rho v_B^2$

The pressure difference is:

$\Delta P = P_A - P_B = \dfrac{1}{2}\rho (v_B^2 - v_A^2)$

Substitute the values:

$\Delta P = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 800 \times (2^2 - 0.5^2)$

$\Delta P = 400 \times (4 - 0.25) = 400 \times 3.75 = 1500 \text{ Pa}$

Answer: $1500 \text{ Pa}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A tiny spherical glass bead is projected vertically downwards into a deep column of highly viscous oil. Its initial downward velocity $v_0$ is twice its terminal velocity ($v_0 = 2v_t$). Which of the following descriptions correctly shows the variation of its velocity ($v$) with time ($t$)?
options: A curve starting at $v_0$ on the velocity axis and decreasing with a continuously flattening slope to approach a horizontal asymptote at $v_t$.
A curve starting at $v_0$ on the velocity axis and decreasing continuously to approach zero asymptotically.
A straight line starting at $v_0$ on the velocity axis and decreasing linearly until it abruptly becomes horizontal at $v_t$.
A curve starting at $v_0$ on the velocity axis and increasing with a continuously flattening slope to approach a higher horizontal asymptote.
questions.solution:
The net downward force on the spherical bead is given by $F_{net} = W_{eff} - F_v$, where $W_{eff}$ is the effective weight (weight minus buoyancy) and $F_v$ is the velocity-dependent viscous drag.

At terminal velocity $v_t$, the net force is zero, so $W_{eff} = 6\pi\eta r v_t$.

The bead is projected with an initial velocity $v_0 = 2v_t$. Since $v_0 \gt v_t$, the initial upward viscous drag is greater than the downward effective weight.

This results in a net upward force, causing the bead to decelerate. As the velocity decreases, the viscous drag decreases, and the net upward force (and thus the retardation) decreases.

The velocity will continuously decrease from $v_0$ and asymptotically approach the terminal velocity $v_t$ from above. The graph is a curve starting at $v_0$ and flattening out to a horizontal asymptote at $v_t$.

Answer: A curve starting at $v_0$ on the velocity axis and decreasing with a continuously flattening slope to approach a horizontal asymptote at $v_t$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II regarding a solid sphere of radius $r$ moving through a fluid.

List-IList-II
(A) Viscous force on a sphere moving at a constant given velocity(I) Proportional to $r^3$
(B) Terminal velocity of a solid sphere falling under gravity(II) Zero
(C) Viscous force on a solid sphere falling at its terminal velocity(III) Proportional to $r$
(D) Viscous drag on a sphere moving in an ideal fluid(IV) Proportional to $r^2$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
According to Stokes' law, the viscous force on a spherical body is $F = 6\pi\eta r v$.
For a constant given velocity $v$, the viscous force $F \propto r$. Thus, (A) matches with (III).

The terminal velocity of a sphere falling under gravity is given by $v_t = \dfrac{2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9\eta}$.
Therefore, terminal velocity $v_t \propto r^2$. Thus, (B) matches with (IV).

The viscous force at terminal velocity is $F = 6\pi\eta r v_t$.
Substituting $v_t \propto r^2$, we get $F \propto r(r^2) = r^3$. Thus, (C) matches with (I).

An ideal fluid is non-viscous ($\eta = 0$). Therefore, the viscous drag is zero. Thus, (D) matches with (II).

The correct matching is (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II).

Answer: (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)

(C) Falling raindrop reaching terminal velocity(III) Atmospheric pressure
(D) Mercury barometer(IV) Stokes' law


Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
A Venturi-meter is a device used to measure the flow speed of an incompressible fluid, and it works on Bernoulli's principle. Hence, (A) matches with (II).

Hydraulic brakes in automobiles operate on Pascal's law, which allows pressure to be transmitted equally throughout the brake fluid. Hence, (B) matches with (I).

A falling raindrop attains a constant terminal velocity due to the viscous drag of air balancing its weight, a phenomenon described by Stokes' law. Hence, (C) matches with (IV).

A mercury barometer is an instrument specifically designed to measure atmospheric pressure. Hence, (D) matches with (III).

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III).

Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)

questions.q: Two small drops of mercury, each of radius $R$, coalesce to form a single large drop. The ratio of the total surface energies before and after the change is
questions.solution:
Radius of one drop of mercury is $R$.
$\therefore \quad$ The volume of one drop $=\frac{4}{3} \pi R^3\therefore$ Total volume of the two drops,

V=2 \times \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3=\frac{8}{3} \pi R^3

Let the radius of the large drop formed be $R^{\prime}$.
The volume of the large drop is also $V$.

\therefore \quad \frac{4}{3} \pi R^{\prime 3}=\frac{8}{3} \pi R^3 \Rightarrow R^{\prime 3}=2 R^3 \Rightarrow R^{\prime}=2^{1 / 3} R \text {. }

Now the surface area of the two drops is

S_1=2 \times 4 \pi R^2=8 \pi R^2

and the surface area of the resultant drop is

S_2=4 \pi R^{\prime 2}=4 \pi 2^{2 / 3} R^2

Let $T$ be the surface tension of mercury. Therefore the surface energy of the two drops before coalescing is

U_1=S_1 T=8 \pi R^2 T

and the surface energy after coalescing,

\begin{gathered}
U_2=S_2 T=2^{2 / 3} \times 4 \pi R^2 T \\
\therefore \quad \frac{U_1}{U_2}=\frac{8 \pi R^2 T}{2^{2 / 3} \times 4 \pi R^2 T}=\frac{2}{2^{2 / 3}}=2^{1 / 3} .
\end{gathered}

questions.q: A stream of a liquid of density $\rho$ flowing horizontally with speed $v$ rushes out of a tube of radius $r$ and hits a vertical wall nearly normally. Assuming that the liquid does not rebound from the wall, the force exerted on the wall by the impact of the liquid is given by
questions.solution:
Cross-sectional area $A=\pi r^2$,
Volume of liquid flowing per second $=A V=\pi r^2 V$
Mass of the liquid flowing out per second $=\pi r^2 v \rho$
Initial momentum of liquid per second
$=$ mass of liquid flowing × Speed of liquid
$=\pi r^2 v \rho \times v=\pi r^2 v^2 \rho$
Since the liquid does not rebound after impact, the momentum after impact is zero.
$\therefore$ Rate of change of momentum $=\pi r^2 v^2 \rho$
According to Newton's second law, the force exerted on wall
$=$ rate of change of momentum $=\pi r^2 \rho v^2$

questions.q: A capillary tube of length $L$ and radius $r$ is connected with another capillary tube of the same length but half the radius in series. Problems of series and parallel combination of pipes can be solved in the similar manner as is done in case of an electrical circuit. The only difference is potential difference is replaced by $\Delta p$ and electrical resistance as, $R_1=\frac{8 \eta L}{\pi r^4}=R$

Electric current is replaced by rate of volume flow $V^{\prime}$.
$\Rightarrow \quad \begin{aligned} p & =V R_1=V R....(i) \\ p^{\prime} & =p=V^{\prime} R_{\text {eq }}=V^{\prime}\left(R_1+R_2\right)=V^{\prime}(R+16 R) \\ & =17 V^{\prime} R\end{aligned}$...(ii)
From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get
$\begin{aligned} V R & =17 V^{\prime} R \\ \Rightarrow \quad V^{\prime} & =\frac{V}{17}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The neck and bottom of a bottle are 3 cm and 15 cm in radius respectively. If the cork is pressed with a force 12 N in the neck of the bottle, then force exerted on the bottom of the bottle is
questions.solution:
Pressure at neck of bottle
$p_1=\frac{F_1}{A_1}=\frac{F_1}{\pi r_1^2}$
Similarly, pressure at bottom of bottle
$p_2=\frac{F_2}{A_2}=\frac{F_2}{\pi r_2^2}$
According to Pascal's law, liquids transmit pressure equal in all directions.
$\therefore\begin{aligned}
\frac{F_1}{\pi r_1^2} & =\frac{F_2}{\pi r_2^2} \\
\frac{12}{\pi(3)^2} & =\frac{F_2}{\pi(15)^2} \\
F_2 & =\frac{12 \times 15 \times 15}{3 \times 3} \\
F_2 & =300 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: 64 spherical rain drops of equal size are falling vertically through air with a terminal velocity $1.5 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$. If these drops coalesce to form a big spherical drop, then terminal velocity of big drop is
questions.solution:
Volume of big drop $=64 \times$ volume of a small drop
$\Rightarrow \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3=64 \times \frac{4}{3} \pi r^3 \Rightarrow R=4 r$
The terminal velocity of spherical rain drop
$\begin{aligned}
& v=\frac{2 r^2(\rho-\sigma)}{9 \eta} \Rightarrow v \propto r^2 \\
\Rightarrow \quad & \frac{v_1}{v_2}=\left(\frac{r}{R}\right)^2=\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^2=\frac{1}{16} \\
\therefore \quad & v_2=16 v_1=16 \times 1.5=24 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A frame made of metallic wire enclosing a surface area $A$ is covered with a soap film. If the area of the frame of metallic wire is reduced by $50 \%$, the energy of the soap film will be changed by
questions.solution:
Surface energy $=$ surface tension × surface area
$E=T \times 2 A$
New surface energy,
$E_1=T \times 2\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)=T \times A\%$ decrease in surface energy
$\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{E-E_1}{E} \times 100 \\
& =\frac{2 T A-T A}{2 T A} \times 100=50 \%
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The potential energy of a molecule on the surface of a liquid compared to one inside the liquid is
questions.solution: When the surface area of a liquid is increased, molecules from the interior of the liquid rise to the surface. As these molecules reach the surface work is done against the cohesive force. This work is stored in the molecules in the form of potential energy. Thus, the potential energy of the molecules lying in the surface is greater than that of the molecules in the interior of the liquid.

Thus, $\quad v_{\text {upper side }} \gt v_{\text {lower side }}$

questions.q: Two glass plates are separated by water. If surface tension of water is 75 dyne/cm and area of each plate wetted by water is $8 \mathrm{~cm}^2$ and the distance between the plates is 0.12 mm , then the force applied to separate the two plates is
questions.solution: The shape of water layer between the two plates is shown in the figure. Thickness $d$ of the film $=0.12 \mathrm{~mm}=0.012 \mathrm{~cm}$ Radius $R$ of the cylindrical face $=\frac{d}{2}$ Pressure difference across the surface $=\frac{T}{R}=\frac{2 T}{d}$ Area of each plate wetted by water $=A$ Force $F$ required to separate the two plates is given by $F=$ pressure difference × area $=\frac{2 T}{d} A$ Putting the given values, we get $F=\frac{2 \times 75 \times 8}{0.012}=10^5$ dyne

questions.q: A raft of wood of mass 120 kg floats in water. The weight that can be put on the raft to make it just sink, should be $\left(d_{\text {raft }}=600 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^3\right)$
questions.solution:
Volume of raft is given by
$V=\frac{m}{d}=\frac{120}{600}=0.2 \mathrm{~m}^3$
If the raft is immersed fully in water.
Then weight of water displaced is $=V d_{\text {water }}=0.2 \times 10^3=200 \mathrm{~kg}$
Hence, the additional weight which is supported by raft
$=200 \mathrm{~kg}-120 \mathrm{~kg}=80 \mathrm{~kg}$
